summary: This best current practice requests an IPv4 /10 block as Shared Address Space for Carrier-Grade NAT devices, to number interfaces between those devices and customer equipment. It is separate from RFC 1918 private space.

plainLanguage.summary: Providers sharing one address among many homes need a special private range. This sets aside a block just for that.

questions: why not use rfc 1918 for cgn
subtitle: A dedicated IPv4 block, 100.64.0.0/10, for the links between carrier-grade NATs and customer routers.

tldr.problem: ISPs that deploy Carrier-Grade NAT need address space for the interfaces between the CGN and customer equipment, but globally unique space is scarce and RFC 1918 space can overlap with the customer's own network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC has IANA allocate an IPv4 /10 as Shared Address Space. It may be used only inside Service Provider networks, and must not be routed or forwarded across provider boundaries.
tldr.outcome: IANA recorded the range 100.64.0.0/10. The document updates RFC 5735, and the IESG note says the IETF remains committed to IPv6.

today: RFC 6598 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 153) and its metadata shows no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 5735 by adding one more special-use IPv4 block, 100.64.0.0/10.

sections.title: Why a New Address Block
sections.content:
IPv4 address space is nearly exhausted, yet ISPs must keep supporting IPv4 growth until IPv6 is fully deployed. Many will deploy a Carrier-Grade NAT (CGN) device. Public address space is expected on those networks and the existing private space causes operational problems there, so ISPs need a new block, the Shared Address Space. It numbers the interfaces that connect CGN devices to Customer Premises Equipment (CPE).

Like RFC 1918 space, it is not globally routable and can be reused by many pieces of equipment. Unlike RFC 1918 space, it has limits: it can only be used in Service Provider networks, or on routing equipment that can translate addresses across interfaces when the addresses are identical on two interfaces.

The RFC asks for a /10. After talking with many ISPs, the authors say a /10 is the smallest block that lets them deploy CGNs on a regional basis without nested CGNs. The document updates RFC 5735.

The IESG note records very rough consensus for the allocation and says that, while this may solve a short-term operational problem, the IETF remains committed to IPv6 deployment.
sections.plainLanguage: Providers are running out of normal addresses but still have to connect customers. They asked for one special range of numbers to use only inside their own networks.

sections.title: The Alternatives
sections.content:
The CGN-to-CPE interfaces could be numbered from four kinds of address space, and the RFC weighs each.

  • Globally unique space: causes the fewest problems but is impractical. The Regional Internet Registries could allocate one /10 shared by all providers, but not a unique assignment for each provider.
  • Usurped (squat) space: providers MUST NOT use it. If advertisements leak, the legitimate holders and those who want to reach them can be harmed, and the provider and its subscribers may lose connectivity to them.
  • RFC 1918 space: usable only if the CPE/NAT is known to work when the same block is on both its inside and outside interfaces, or if the block used is known not to be used on the subscriber side.
  • Shared Address Space: the choice when neither RFC 1918 condition holds, which is typically the case in an unmanaged service where subscribers bring their own CPE.
sections.plainLanguage: There are four kinds of numbers a provider could use. Real ones are too scarce, stolen ones are not allowed, the home-style ones can clash with the customer's own numbers, so a new special range is the safe choice.

sections.title: Rules for Using Shared Address Space
sections.content:
The block is for Service Provider use to facilitate CGN deployment. It may also serve as extra non-globally-routable space on equipment that can translate addresses when identical ranges appear on two interfaces. Devices MUST be able to do that translation.

Packets with Shared Address Space source or destination addresses MUST NOT be forwarded across Service Provider boundaries, and providers MUST filter them on ingress links. The exception is business relationships such as hosted CGN services.

For DNS, providers MUST NOT put Shared Address Space in zone files (in external-facing zone files if they run split DNS). Reverse queries for these addresses MUST NOT be forwarded to the global DNS, and DNS providers SHOULD filter them on recursive nameservers. This avoids needing something like the AS112 service that exists for RFC 1918 reverse queries (RFC 6304).

Anyone using the block for something other than CGN service is likely to have trouble when they run out of public IPv4 addresses and need to connect to CGN service, because CGN needs non-overlapping address space on each side of the home NAT and the CGN.
sections.plainLanguage: The special numbers stay inside the provider's own building. They must never be sent out to the wider internet, and the public phone book must not list them.

sections.title: Risks and Measured Impacts
sections.content:
Some applications look up the outside address of their CPE and behave differently if it is a special-use address. If CPE outside interfaces are numbered from a newly reserved block, some of these applications may fail. The usual assumption that a non-special-use address is reachable from the Internet is generally safe but not always true, for example behind a CGN.

The RFC lists services hurt by CGNs: console gaming, video streaming, peer-to-peer seeding, geo-location, sites that limit simultaneous logins per public address, and 6to4. It cites testing in a work-in-progress document to say the impacts on the first five are comparable whether globally unique, Shared Address Space or RFC 1918 addresses are used.

6to4 differs. Per RFC 6343, CPE routers do not try to start 6to4 tunnels when configured with RFC 1918 or RFC 5735 WAN addresses, but may try with globally unique or Shared Address Space addresses, and that would fail. Providers can mitigate this, and because the Shared range is well defined, CPE vendors can add it to their special-use address lists. Providers told the authors that overlapping RFC 1918 space on both sides of the CPE is harder to mitigate than the 6to4 effect.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs guess whether they can be reached from the outside by looking at their address. A new special range can confuse a few of them, but the other choices cause confusion too.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Like other special-use IPv4 addresses in RFC 5735, Shared Address Space raises no direct security issues, but the Internet does not inherently protect against abuse of these addresses, and attacks have relied on unexpected use of similar special-use addresses. Operators should consider adding the block to ingress filter lists (RFC 3704) unless their service incorporates a CGN.

Except for hosted CGN service or similar business relationships, routing information about Shared Address Space MUST NOT cross Service Provider boundaries and incoming advertisements MUST be filtered. Packets MUST NOT be forwarded across boundaries and MUST be filtered on ingress, the block MUST NOT appear in external-facing DNS zone files, and reverse queries MUST NOT go to the global DNS. DNS providers SHOULD filter such reverse queries on recursive nameservers.
sections.plainLanguage: Keep the special numbers locked inside the provider. Do not announce them, forward them or list them in public directories.

sections.title: The Allocation
sections.content: IANA has recorded the allocation of an IPv4 /10 for Shared Address Space. The range is 100.64.0.0/10.
sections.plainLanguage: The official keeper of address lists wrote down the special range, so now everyone knows which numbers it is.

The fallback, typical for unmanaged service
